description: A drawn frame of capped honeycomb is held up and turned so light passes straight through the wax, every sealed cell reading amber-translucent against the open air, three workers crossing the face unhurried, a strip of old bicycle inner tube holding a hairline crack in the frame's corner together.

A drawn frame dense with capped brood and honey both is lifted clear and angled, the brood cells reading pale and domed at the centre, the honey arc above them translucent, a single wax scale stuck flat to the back of a thumb gripping the lug.

A drawn frame still threaded with propolis along its top bar is lifted free and turned face-on, the comb bowing very slightly with its own weight, bees walking steadily across the sealed surface, a goose-feather brush hooked over the box rim below.

A drawn frame built out to the very edge of the timber is raised slowly, its comb so full it trembles, light passing through the upper honey band in one translucent arc, a chipped enamel mug standing forgotten on the roof of the hive behind it.

A tin smoker with a leather bellows breathes one slow white curl low across the open top bars of a hive, the bees parting where the smoke touches them, the smoker's lid tipped on its edge in the grass, a pair of gloves left inside-out beside it.

A tin smoker with a patched bellows sits on the corner of a hive, one last rope of white smoke unraveling across the top bars and dissolving, the bellows creased and darkened from long use, a brick turned on its side holding the adjoining lid weighted down.

A tin smoker with a dented body and a riveted spout breathes a thin continuous thread of smoke over an open brood box, the bees fanning gently beneath it, a stub of dry grass still trailing from the smoker's spout, a saucer of water with a flat cork floating in it set nearby for the bees to drink.

A warmed uncapping knife is drawn down the face of a fully capped frame, the cut wax peeling away in one pale continuous sheet that folds softly into the tray below, the exposed cells immediately beginning to weep, a hive tool worn silver-bright along one edge resting across the tray's rim.

A sheet of uncapped wax lies curled in the bottom of a wide settling tray, still holding the exact shape of the comb it came from, honey pooling beneath it, a small sprig of dried herb tucked under the twine of a nearby wax-sealed jar on the bench.

The extractor's small brass tap is opened and a single unbroken amber thread of honey falls in a slow arc into a wide-mouthed jar below, the thread thickening and thinning as the drum slows, a coil of spare wire left on the bench beside the jar.

A lifted honey super is set down across an upturned hive lid, its frames standing in their rack, bees walking the top bars in slow deliberate lines, the propolis between the frames drawn into fine threads where they were parted, a goose-feather brush lying flat across one end of the super.

The top bars of an open brood box are exposed, bees flowing across them in a slow continuous current, each bee pausing briefly then moving on, the frames packed so tightly the bees must climb over one another, a chipped enamel mug perched on the corner of the box beside the open hive.

A lifted super rests on its side in the grass, its frames still in place, propolis-dark along the runners, bees circling the exposed edges and re-landing, a strip of old bicycle inner tube wrapped twice around one cracked box corner to hold it closed.

A swarm hangs from a low apple branch in one dense living teardrop, the cluster as large as two fists pressed together, a clean white sheet spread on the grass directly beneath it, a plain timber box held up under the mass to coax the cluster down, the mass made entirely of living bees layered over one another, its whole surface small clinging bodies and folded wings.

A swarm cluster clings to a low plum branch, its outer surface rippling slowly as bees adjust and resettle, the branch bowed very slightly under the collective weight, a straw skep held up beneath it with both arms fully extended, a goose-feather brush resting across its mouth, the mass made entirely of living bees layered over one another, its whole surface small clinging bodies and folded wings.

A swarm hangs from a forked elder branch in a dense rounded mass, the bees on the outside fanning in slow unison, a white linen sheet laid beneath to catch any that fall, a timber box with a plain painted bee on its side lifted up to receive the cluster, the mass made entirely of living bees layered over one another, its whole surface small clinging bodies and folded wings.

A living bee-beard covers the lower front panel and landing board of a hive, hundreds of workers fanning together in one shaggy curtain that shifts and breathes as a whole, the hive's plain painted surface visible above the cluster, a saucer of water with a cork float set on the ground before them.

A bee-beard of workers hangs from the landing board in a dense living bib, the individual bees barely distinguishable in the mass, the whole thing swaying fractionally, a brick turned on its side propping the hive's lid ajar above.

A domed straw skep is being lifted out of its stone-wall alcove, the straw coils dark and smooth from many seasons of use, bees clustering at its entrance as it rises, a hive tool worn silver-bright on one edge slipped into a back pocket.

A hollow-log hive lashed in the fork of an old pear tree has its timber plug drawn slowly out, bees beginning to emerge along the plug's edges before it is fully clear, propolis sealing the gap having cracked and peeled in long translucent strips.

A squat glass jar of just-spun honey stands on a shed windowsill, light passing straight through it so the honey reads brilliant amber all the way to the base, the jar plain and unadorned, sealed with wax and tied with twine, a small sprig tucked under the knot.

A wide-mouthed glass jar of fresh honey sits on a workbench, air bubbles rising through it in a slow chain, the honey reading translucent at its upper edge and deeper amber at its core, a saucer with a flat cork floating in water beside it.

A pale block of filtered beeswax has been turned out of its tin mould onto a bare bench, its surface still carrying the faint impression of the mould's seam, the wax opaque at its thick centre and translucent at the thin edges, a pair of gloves left inside-out on the bench beside it.

A row of freshly rolled beeswax candles lies on a cloth to cool, each one still faintly ridged from the honeycomb sheet it was rolled from, the ridges casting a fine regular texture across the surface, a single wax scale resting on the cloth beside the last candle.

A bare timber frame is clamped to a bench, three of its four sides already strung with fine wire pulled taut, the fourth side waiting, a coil of wire and a pair of pliers laid beside it, a hive tool worn silver-bright on one edge propped against the bench leg.

A drawn frame of capped honeycomb stands propped upright against the side of an open hive, the light coming through the wax from behind so every sealed cell reads amber-translucent, a dozen workers walking the face, a flat stone steadying the frame's foot in the grass.

A drawn frame of capped comb rests in a timber carrying rack beside the open hive, angled just enough that light passes through the upper honey band in one bright translucent arc, bees moving unhurried across the wax, a goose-feather brush laid across the rack's end.

A drawn frame leans in the open mouth of an empty super set down on the grass, light coming clean through the honey band so the wax reads amber all the way across, a few workers walking the cells, a chipped enamel mug standing on the box beside it.
